title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century
abstract: The main driver of inequality--returns on capital that exceed the rate of economic growth--is again threatening to generate extreme discontent and undermine democratic values. Thomas Piketty's findings in this ambitious, original, rigorous work will transform debate and set the agenda for the next generation of thought about wealth and inequality.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Thomas Piketty’s Capital in the Twenty-First Century has become a major reference point in contemporary scholarship on inequality and political economy. With 13,766 OpenAlex citations and top 1% citation standing for its field and year, the book has not only been widely read but also repeatedly used as evidence-bearing reference in later research. Its influence extends beyond academia into teaching, policy-oriented discussion, and formal book review literature.

Full narrative

Published by Harvard University Press in 2014, Capital in the Twenty-First Century quickly established itself as a foundational work in debates over wealth concentration, inequality, and democracy. The record shows sustained scholarly uptake across a broad range of fields, especially economics, political economy, social policy, and inequality studies. The citation profile is especially strong and geographically wide, with substantial use across the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, Canada, and other national research communities.

The book’s impact is not limited to being frequently cited in a general sense. Scite reports 27 supporting citation statements, indicating that later authors have explicitly relied on its claims, data, or framing in their own arguments. At the same time, the presence of a small number of contradicting statements suggests that the book has also served as a point of active scholarly debate rather than passive consensus. That mix is typical of a work that has helped set an agenda: it is used, tested, and argued with.

The citing literature shows especially strong concentration in economics and related policy fields, but also in interdisciplinary areas such as housing, finance, neoliberalism, social reform, and political economy and Marxism. Recent citing works continue to draw on the book in discussions of wealth inequality, market power, fiscal sustainability, and the political implications of inequality, showing that its core concerns remain live in current research. Formal reviews in venues such as the Journal of Political Economy and the Journal of Economic Inequality further underscore the book’s status as a serious scholarly intervention.

Teaching adoption also appears substantial. The book is listed in multiple MIT OpenCourseWare reading lists and appears in recorded or promotional educational materials associated with TED and Harvard University Press, indicating that it functions as a pedagogical anchor as well as a research reference. Library subject classifications and Open Library holdings show that it is collected under themes including capitalism, wealth, inequality, democracy, and social welfare, which aligns with its broad interdisciplinary reach. The available record does not include event archives or download totals, so those forms of reception cannot be assessed here; what can be said confidently is that the book has achieved durable scholarly, educational, and policy relevance.
